Body of myths and genre of folklore originating among the ancient Greeks, concerning the origin and nature of the world, the lives of deities and heroes, and the significance of cult and ritual practices. Together with [[Roman mythology]] it forms classical mythology. Modern scholars study the myths for what they reveal about the religious and political institutions of [[Ancient Greece]] and about mythmaking itself.

The myths were first transmitted in an oral-poetic tradition, most likely by Minoan and Mycenaean singers beginning in the 18th century BC. The myths of the heroes of the Trojan War and its aftermath became part of the oral tradition behind [[Homer]]'s epic poems, the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*. [[Hesiod]]'s *Theogony* and *Works and Days* contain accounts of the genesis of the world, the succession of divine rulers, the human ages, and the origin of sacrificial practices. Myths also survive in the Homeric Hymns, the Epic Cycle, lyric poetry, fifth-century BC drama, and Hellenistic and Roman-era writers such as Plutarch and Pausanias.

Pictorial evidence is equally important. Vase paintings, votive gifts, and other artifacts depict gods, heroes, and mythic episodes; geometric pottery of the eighth century BC shows scenes from the Epic Cycle and the adventures of [[Heracles]].

The Olympian gods, who reside on [[Mount Olympus]] under [[Zeus]], include Poseidon, Hades, Hera, Athena, and Apollo. Heroes such as Heracles and Theseus, slayer of the [[Minotaur]], serve as intermediaries between gods and humans. The myths have had an extensive influence on the culture, arts, and literature of Western civilization.

Mixture of [[Sulfur|sulfur]], [[Charcoal|charcoal]], and [[Potassium nitrate|potassium nitrate]] (saltpeter), and the earliest known chemical explosive. It is also called black powder. The sulfur and charcoal act as fuels, while the saltpeter is an oxidizer.

Gunpowder is classified as a low explosive: it deflagrates, burning at subsonic speeds, whereas high explosives detonate and produce a supersonic shockwave. When ignited behind a projectile it generates enough pressure to force the shot from the muzzle at high speed, but usually not enough to rupture the barrel. It has therefore served widely as a propellant in [[Firearm|firearms]], [[Artillery|artillery]], rocketry, and pyrotechnics, and as a blasting agent in quarrying, mining, and the building of pipelines, tunnels, and roads. Its low brisance suits it to blasting slate and monumental stone. Combustion converts less than half of its mass to gas; the residue fouls barrels and corrodes wrought iron and steel, so gunpowder arms need regular cleaning.

The first confirmed reference to what can be considered gunpowder in China dates to the 9th century, during the [[Tang dynasty]], in a formula of six parts sulfur, six parts saltpeter, and one part birthwort herb in the *Taishang Shengzu Jindan Mijue* (808). Daoist alchemists seeking an elixir of life probably discovered it by accident; its Chinese name, *huoyao*, means "fire medicine." It was first used for warfare around AD 904. The earliest chemical formula appears in the *Wujing Zongyao*, a [[Song dynasty]] military text written by Zeng Gongliang between 1040 and 1044. High explosives came into use in the second half of the 19th century, and smokeless powder replaced gunpowder in weapons, while [[Dynamite|dynamite]] and ammonium nitrate/fuel oil replaced it in industry.

Indian empire of the classical period, existing from the mid-3rd to the mid-6th century AD. At its peak the dynasty, founded by a king named Gupta, ruled much of the northern [[Indian subcontinent]].

The dynasty's homeland is uncertain. Eastern [[Uttar Pradesh]], Magadha (Bihar), and Bengal have each been proposed. Early rulers were Gupta, his son Ghatotkacha, and Chandragupta I; the Allahabad Pillar inscription calls the first two Maharaja ("Great King") and Chandragupta I Maharajadhiraja ("King of Great Kings"). The high points of the period came under [[Samudragupta]], [[Chandragupta II]], Kumaragupta I, and Skandagupta.

The era produced scholars including [[Kalidasa]], [[Aryabhata]], Varahamihira, and Vatsyayana, who made significant advances in many fields. The [[Mahabharata]] and *Ramayana* were canonized, and the Puranas are thought to have been committed to writing around this time. Architecture, sculpture, and painting of the period "set standards of form and taste [that] determined the whole subsequent course of art, not only in India but far beyond her borders." The rulers followed Hinduism, and Brahmins flourished, but the Guptas were tolerant of other faiths. The period is sometimes described as Pax Gupta and has been considered a Golden Age of India by some historians, a characterization others dispute.

The empire declined after its own former feudatories took much of its territory and authority, and after invasions by the Huna peoples (Kidarites and Alchon Huns) from [[Central Asia]]. After its collapse in the 6th century, India was again ruled by numerous regional kingdoms.

Spectrum of conditions caused by infection with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), a retrovirus that attacks the [[Immune system|immune system]]. Without treatment, HIV infection can progress to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).

HIV spreads primarily through unprotected sex, contaminated needles, [[Blood transfusion|blood transfusions]], and from mother to child during pregnancy, delivery, or breastfeeding. Saliva, sweat, and tears do not transmit it. Initial infection may bring no symptoms or an influenza-like illness 2–4 weeks after exposure. A prolonged stage of clinical latency follows, lasting from about three years to over 20 years without treatment (on average, about eight years). Eventually the infection raises the risk of opportunistic infections such as [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]] and of tumors rare in people with normal immune function. Without treatment, life expectancy is around 11 years.

There is no cure or [[Vaccine|vaccine]], but antiretroviral treatment, taken for life, suppresses the virus to undetectable levels and can extend [[Life expectancy|life expectancy]] to a nearly standard level. A person with an undetectable viral load has effectively no risk of transmitting HIV sexually, a message campaigns by UNAIDS have communicated as "Undetectable = Untransmittable." Prevention includes safe sex, pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis, and needle exchange programs.

HIV passed from other [[Primate|primates]] to humans in west-central Africa in the early-to-mid-20th century. AIDS was first recognized by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in 1981, and its cause was identified in the early part of that decade. The disease is estimated to have caused at least 42.3 million deaths through 2024. In 2025, 1.2 million people acquired HIV and an estimated 40.9 million were living with it. It is considered a [[Pandemic|pandemic]] and has been a source of discrimination and large economic costs.

Protein filament that grows from follicles in the dermis of the skin, one of the distinguishing characteristics of [[Mammal|mammals]]. Human skin, apart from areas such as the palms and soles, produces thick terminal hair and fine vellus hair.

The word refers to two structures. The follicle, which lies in the dermis, contains [[Stem cell|stem cells]] that regrow the hair after it falls out and also help regrow skin after a wound. The shaft, the part above the skin, consists of dead, keratinized cells and has no biochemical activity. Keratin, a [[Protein|protein]], makes up most of its volume, notably alpha-keratin. The shaft has three layers: the outer [[Cuticle|cuticle]], of overlapping flat cells; the cortex, which holds the keratin bundles and is the main source of mechanical strength; and the medulla, an open, unstructured center that is not always present. The shape of the follicle determines the shape of the fiber: straight hair has round fibers, while oval fibers are generally wavy or curly. Arrector pili muscles make hairs stand up, producing goose bumps.

All natural hair colors come from two types of [[Melanin|melanin]]. Eumelanin dominates in brown and black hair and pheomelanin in red hair; blond hair has little pigmentation, and gray hair results when melanin production decreases or stops. Hair grows in cycles of active growth (anagen), regression (catagen), and rest (telogen). In mammals it insulates, protects the skin, aids sensation through [[Whiskers|whiskers]], and may serve in [[Camouflage|camouflage]].

Attitudes toward hair, including [[Hairstyle|hairstyles]] and hair removal, vary across cultures and periods, and hair often signals a person's beliefs or social position, such as age, gender, or religion.

Sixth [[Amorites|Amorite]] king of [[Babylon]] (r. c. 1792–c. 1750 BC), also spelled Hammurapi. He succeeded his father, Sin-muballit.

During his reign he conquered the kingdoms of Larsa, Eshnunna, and Mari, bringing almost all of [[Mesopotamia]] under Babylonian rule. Babylon rose under him to the status of a leading kingdom of the Middle East, and the foundations were laid for it to become one of the major cities of ancient history. The most common translation of his name is "the ancestor is great," though the meaning is debated; an alternative Amorite reading is "the ancestor heals."

He is best known for his law code, said to have been inspired by Shamash, the Babylonian god of justice. The [[Code of Hammurabi]] is one of the oldest legal texts discovered and the longest to survive from the ancient Near East. It comprises 282 laws inscribed in Akkadian on a black diorite stele 2.25 m tall. The stele originally stood in a temple in Sippar, was taken as booty to [[Susa]], and was rediscovered in 1901.

His reign is among the best documented in Mesopotamia. The sources are mostly [[Cuneiform|cuneiform]] texts on clay tablets and stone, written in Babylonian and Sumerian, including royal inscriptions and correspondence unearthed at Larsa and Mari. The Mari archives cover the 18th to 32nd years of his reign (1774 to 1761 BC), the best-understood period.

His son Samsu-iluna succeeded him but failed to maintain the empire. Later tradition de-emphasized Hammurabi's military achievements and made his role as the ideal lawgiver the main part of his legacy. Archaeologists rediscovered him in the late 19th century, and he has since been seen as an important figure in the history of law.

Imperial dynasty of China (202 BC–AD 220), founded by Liu Bang after the collapse of the [[Qin dynasty]]. It is divided into the Western Han (202 BC–AD 9), with its capital at Chang'an (modern [[Xi'an]]), and the Eastern Han (AD 25–220), interrupted by the Xin dynasty (AD 9–23) of the usurping regent Wang Mang. It ended in 220 when Cao Pi, king of Wei, usurped the throne from Emperor Xian, and was followed by the [[Three Kingdoms]] period. It is considered a golden age of Chinese history; the majority ethnic group of modern China calls itself the "Han people," and Chinese writing is called "Han characters."

The empire was divided into commanderies under the central government and semi-autonomous kingdoms, which gradually lost their autonomy. From the reign of Emperor Wu (r. 141–87 BC) the court officially sponsored [[Confucianism]] in education and politics. The government nationalized the salt and iron industries in 117 BC to finance military campaigns. Advances included papermaking, rudders for ships, negative numbers, raised-relief maps, hydraulic-powered armillary spheres, and seismometers.

The [[Xiongnu]] defeated the Han in 200 BC, leading to a policy of marriage alliance and tribute. From 133 BC Emperor Wu campaigned against them, taking the Hexi Corridor and the Tarim Basin and helping to establish the [[Silk Road]]. He also annexed Nanyue in 111 BC and Dian in 109 BC, and in 108 BC conquered Gojoseon in northern Korea.

After AD 92, palace [[Eunuch|eunuchs]] became involved in violent court power struggles with consort clans. Taoist societies led the Yellow Turban Rebellion. After Emperor Ling died (r. 168–189), officers massacred the eunuchs, and military governors became warlords who divided the empire.

Positive mental state ranging from contentment to intense joy, closely linked to well-being and life satisfaction.

There is no single accepted definition, and usage differs by culture and context. The word is used mainly in two ways: for the current experience of an emotion such as pleasure or joy (Daniel Kahneman: "what I experience here and now"), and for an appraisal of life satisfaction (Ruut Veenhoven: "overall appreciation of one's life as-a-whole"). Subjective well-being combines both, and the Greek term *eudaimonia* is variously translated as happiness, flourishing, or blessedness. Results depend on the definition: Nordic countries often score highest on surveys of subjective well-being, while [[South America|South American]] countries score higher on surveys of current positive experience. Philosopher Michela Summa distinguishes joy, bound to the present moment, from happiness, which presupposes an evaluation of one's life.

In 1780 the English utilitarian philosopher [[Jeremy Bentham]] proposed measuring happiness to judge how well a government performed. Today it is measured mainly by self-report surveys, which are prone to cognitive biases such as the peak–end rule; memories of felt emotions can be inaccurate, and people predict their future emotions poorly. Scales include the four-item Subjective Happiness Scale (1999), the 20-item Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (1988), and the Cantril ladder, on which respondents rate their lives from 0 to 10 and which is used in the World Happiness Report.

Twin studies estimate the heritability of happiness at 30–50% of variance, and people adapt quickly to life events, a process called the hedonic treadmill.

Condition of physical and emotional well-being, commonly understood as the normal functioning of a living being, free of [[Disease|disease]], pain, or injury.

Definitions of health have varied by purpose and over time. In 1948 the [[World Health Organization]] (WHO) proposed a broader definition: "physical, mental, and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease and infirmity." Critics called it vague, excessively broad, and unmeasurable. In the 1980s the WHO fostered the health promotion movement, and in 1984 it revised the definition to describe health as "a resource for everyday life, not the objective of living," emphasizing resilience and social and personal resources as well as physical capacities.

Factors known as determinants of health include gender, ethnic background, lifestyle, economic status, and genetics. Observers differ on emphasis: some stress individual choices and high-risk behaviors, while others stress structural determinants, such as unequal access to health care. Health can be promoted by [[Exercise|exercise]] and adequate [[Sleep|sleep]] and by avoiding [[Smoking|smoking]] and excessive stress.

Public health measures such as vaccination, sanitation, and antibiotics have controlled many infectious diseases. The eradication of [[Smallpox|smallpox]] in 1980 was achieved through coordinated global vaccination and surveillance. Contemporary debates include the rise of obesity and metabolic disorders and the relative roles of personal behavior and social conditions; [[Public health]] addresses health at the level of populations.

Improvement or maintenance of health through the prevention, diagnosis, treatment, amelioration, or cure of disease, illness, injury, and other physical and mental impairments.

It is delivered by health professionals and allied health fields, including [[Medicine|medicine]], [[Dentistry|dentistry]], pharmacy, midwifery, [[Nursing|nursing]], optometry, audiology, psychology, occupational therapy, physical therapy, and athletic training. The term covers primary, secondary, and tertiary care, mental health care, and public health.

Primary care is the first point of consultation within the system and supports accessible, continuous, comprehensive, and coordinated care for patients of all ages. Providers include general practitioners, family physicians, physician assistants, nurse practitioners. Patients may be referred for secondary or tertiary care. Primary care treats chronic illnesses such as hypertension, diabetes, and asthma and provides maternal and child services including vaccination. In the United States, the 2013 National Health Interview Survey found skin disorders (42.7%) and osteoarthritis and joint disorders (33.6%) to be the most common reasons for seeing a physician.

Access varies across countries, communities, and individuals. Barriers include financial limits such as insurance coverage, geographic and logistical obstacles, and personal limitations such as poor health literacy. These barriers reduce the use of medical services and the efficacy of treatment. According to the [[World Health Organization]], a well-functioning system requires financing, a well-trained and adequately paid workforce, reliable information, and well-maintained facilities. Health systems range from predominantly public models to market-oriented ones, and global health expenditure reached about $9.8 trillion in 2021, roughly 10% of world GDP. Critics note that spending correlates weakly with outcomes such as life expectancy. The eradication of [[Smallpox|smallpox]] in 1980 was the first elimination of a disease by deliberate health care intervention.
